_comment: Lantern charge and knockdown/revive tuning. Charge existed in the scaffold but never drained, which made the solo Anchor Revive free - it is paid for with 'a full lantern charge', and a charge that never depletes costs nothing. Values are placeholders for Chris.

charge._note: 0 means the lantern never runs out. Chris's call, 2026-10-20: "i don't think the lantern should ever run out of light, its kind of a hurt to run out and then be all like running around like that. the risk is always having it on." Light costs local safety: machines notice it, relics need it, and it leaves fewer dark places to hide. A fuel gauge would make a dry lantern a second failure state on top of the weather.
charge._anchorRevivePrice: RESOLVED, row 73: once per run is the price. The Anchor Revive consumes chargesPerRun (1) and emits a local distress pulse for the revive duration. It never accelerates zone pressure. Not a fuel cost: with light unlimited, spending a lantern cell would strand a player lightless for the rest of the run.
charge._rechargeProposal: PROPOSAL, default off, Chris's call: refill the lantern when you bank at the relay. It would make the relay do double duty - securing loot and buying more light - which strengthens the bank-or-push decision. It also softens the charge economy, so it is off until Chris says otherwise.

knockdown._note: Enemies knock Lightkeepers down rather than killing them. A downed player keeps their loot until the crew wipes.
knockdown._dropsCarriedCrateNote: Chris's call, 2026-10-20: a downed Lightkeeper keeps the crate, matching the note above - you keep your loot until the crew wipes. Was true, which did nothing useful: the flag only cleared the carry slot, so the crate still extracted at full value. If this is ever set back to true, RunStateService.knockDown must also remove RestorationCrates from state.haul.carried, or the drop is cosmetic again. DECISIONS.md row 59 now also depends on this flag: with dropsCarriedCrate false and downedWalkSpeed 0, a crate cannot be banked while its carrier is down, which is what physically enforces 'everyone protects the carrier'. Setting this true would let a crew abandon the carrier and still extract the crate, removing that enforcement.
knockdown._bleedOutNote: 0 = downed players wait indefinitely. The handoff's forgiving tone argues against a bleed-out timer in v1; the wipe already comes from the whole crew going down. Set a value only if playtests show downs are being ignored.

revive._note: Server-validated hold. Moving out of range cancels it, so reviving is a real commitment of a teammate's attention - that is the co-op role the handoff asks for.

sweeperContact._note: First-slice rule: a Sweeper pressures, telegraphs, searches and interferes with stock; it does not freeze a solo player in place. Contact remains a readable threat seam for later enemy-specific consequences, but this maintenance machine is not a containment enemy.
sweeperContact._hitsNote: hitsToKnockDown with decay is what makes one Sweeper survivable and four lethal, without giving players a health bar to optimise.

light._comment: ADDED 2026-10-29, Chris's call: 'the actual reach must be portable, tunable, and shared by light visibility/enemy logic later'. These five keys were a C++ placeholder on ULLKLanternLightComponent until now, which put the most consequential number in the game - how far a keeper can see - in a file the balance tests cannot read. Mesh placement and cosmetic flicker stay in Content; the inner cone angle stays in code because it is edge softness, not reach.
light._radiusNote: THE NUMBER THIS BLOCK EXISTS FOR. Read against data/enemies.json: aggroRadiusDark is 12 and aggroRadiusLit is 38, so at 30 a lit keeper is noticed from 8 studs BEYOND the edge of their own light. That asymmetry is row 5's trade made physical - light reveals value and attracts danger, and the danger arrives from the dark you just announced yourself to. Raising this above 38 inverts it: you would see patrols before they aggro, and light would become pure advantage. 30 was the placeholder's value and is kept as the initial data value rather than retuned in the same change that moved it.
light._coneNote: The OUTER cone of the electric lantern's working aperture. It is deliberately broad enough to read as a hooded carried source rather than a flashlight beam, while still leaving darkness outside the keeper's chosen direction. The inner cone is deliberately NOT here - it only softens the falloff and changes nothing about reach.
light._intensityNote: Unreal candelas. Tuned in the enclosed walk lab under the current Lumen baseline: 250cd read as a flashlight and overexposed nearby relics; 25cd gives a carried electric lantern a readable pool without whitening the room. Intensity is visual-only: detectability and gameplay reach are authored separately, so this can be tuned by eye without changing enemy balance.
light._intensityWas6: FIXED 2026-10-29, Chris's report: 'i don't see the lantern turning on or off, i tried in shadows to see'. The light WAS toggling - 6 was simply invisible. ULocalLightComponent defaults to Unitless with Intensity 5000, so an unpinned 6 was 6 on a scale whose normal value is five thousand, roughly 800x too dim, and the only reason it looked like a broken toggle is that nothing logged the toggle. Both halves of that are fixed: the unit is pinned and every state change now logs.
light._colorNote: Linear RGB, 0-1, alpha deliberately absent - a light has no opacity and an authored alpha would be a field that silently does nothing. Warm because every other light in this game is the storm, and the keeper's lantern should read as the one human thing in the building.
light._shadowNote: On, and load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Row 5 is about what you reveal, and revealed geometry with no shadow reads as flat - you cannot tell a shelf from a painted wall, which is exactly the judgement looting asks for. If this is ever turned off for performance, the store stops being readable before it stops being pretty.

movement._note: Movement is a readability and route-choice tool, not a stamina minigame. Sprint gets you to an exit or away from a Sweeper; crouch gives players a deliberate slow mode for tight shops and careful approach. Neither changes zone pressure.
